note: Usually the first building block in any system design answer. Know the common algorithms (round robin, least connections, consistent hashing) and where a load balancer sits - in front of your app servers, not your database.

The single highest-leverage answer to 'how would you make this faster' in almost every design interview. Know cache-aside vs write-through, and be ready to discuss eviction policies (LRU) and cache invalidation.
How you split one database into many once a single machine can't hold or serve all your data. Know the common sharding keys and the real tradeoff: cross-shard queries and joins get much harder.

How you copy data across multiple machines for availability and read scaling. Know the difference between leader-follower (primary-replica) setups and the replication-lag tradeoff that comes with them.

A distributed system can't give you Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance all at once - network partitions are a fact of life, so the real question interviewers want is: does your system favor C or A when one happens?
The standard way to decouple two services so a slow or failing consumer doesn't take down the producer. Know when you'd reach for a queue (async work, buffering spikes) versus a direct API call.

How static content gets served from a server physically close to the user instead of your origin server every time. Know what belongs on a CDN (images, video, static assets) and what doesn't (personalized, frequently-changing data).

How an API protects itself from being overwhelmed by one client, whether by accident or on purpose. Know the common algorithms - token bucket and sliding window come up most - and where you'd enforce it (gateway vs. per-service).

The technique that lets you add or remove servers from a distributed cache or database without having to re-shuffle almost all of your data - the detail that separates a strong distributed-systems answer from a shaky one.

Less a technical question than a judgment one - interviewers want to see you weigh the real tradeoffs (deployment independence and fault isolation vs. operational complexity and network overhead), not just declare microservices 'better.'
